title: Realtime Resharding, KV Population, and NCCL Heuristics — Sketch
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note collects a working set of ideas and heuristics for performing online re-sharding and KV-cache population in Redwood's multi-GPU serving runtime. Focus is on minimizing tail latency and cross-GPU communication during steady state and during scale/placement events (node preemption, autoscale, rolling upgrades). It intentionally mixes kernel-level considerations (fusion, pipelining) with higher-level scheduling heuristics and NCCL tuning knobs because those layers interact in meaningful ways for production SLOs.

Background / motivating incidents:
- Recent incident (JIRA-RT-1987) where a rolling upgrade + opportunistic scaling caused a transient 4–6x tail latency spike for 8→16 replica autoscale due to naive eager KV rebalancing and NCCL all-gather saturation.
- Benchmarks show that naive sharding swap for large KV entries (many thousands of tokens) can saturate PCIe/NVLink for several hundred ms, producing request timeouts for concurrent low-latency calls.

High-level goals (SLO-driven):
- End-user p50 latency should be unchanged by background resharding work.
- P99 increase limited to <= 1.5x baseline when rebalancing under controlled conditions.
- Allow capacity changes (add/remove GPU) with minimal blocking of request processing.
- Ensure correctness: KV consistency (no stale cache reads when re-assignment completes).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Models use autoregressive decoding with KV cache per request. KV entries are sharded across GPUs by contiguous head/feature ranges in our typical tensor-parallel layout.
- Network topology varies (intra-node NVLink + inter-node PCIe or InfiniBand). NCCL behavior differs by topology.
- We cannot rely on dedicated maintenance windows for many customers; rebalancing must be online.
- Storage for warm/cold KV snapshots is available (local SSD + central object store) but restoring from central store is slower than NVLink copy.

Terminology:
- eager-reshard: move entire KV shard immediately on topology change before accepting new requests routed to new layout.
- lazy-reshard (on-demand): leave KV in old location and fetch/forward on first access; proactively migrate hot prefixes asynchronously.
- KV population: process of filling target-shard KV entries so that subsequent accesses are local.
- bulk-copy window: controlled period where we throttle/give bandwidth budget to rebalancing traffic.

Design options considered:
1) Strict eager re-shard (blocking):
   - On topology change, quiesce new request routing, move all KV shards to new owners, restart/route.
   - Pros: simple, correctness trivial, no request-time remote KV fetches.
   - Cons: long blocking time; saturates interconnect; poor UX for autoscale.

2) Lazy on-demand + opportunistic prefetch: (preferred baseline)
   - Keep existing KV placement; when a request arrives and its token prefix maps to a non-local shard, perform small remote fetch (RPC) for the required KV frames and continue decoding. Concurrently record hot prefixes and backfill them to the new owner in the background.
   - Prefetch heuristics (see below) guide background migration.
   - Pros: no long blocking; fast warm-up for steady hotspots; amortizes background cost.
   - Cons: requires remote fetch path; slightly higher p50 for cold requests unless prefetch succeeds.

3) Hybrid windowed bulk-copy + lazy fallback:
   - When scaling rapidly (adding many GPUs), do a short, bandwidth-limited bulk-copy for the top-K hot prefixes (by request volume) while leaving the long tail lazy. After the window, remaining prefixes served remote-on-demand.
   - Pros: captures most real traffic cheaply, limits worst-case rebalancing bandwidth.

Prefetch / prioritization heuristics:
- Priority score for prefix P on shard S = alpha * recent_qps(P) + beta * estimated_future_qps(P, model) - gamma * estimated_migration_cost(P,S).
- recent_qps: exponentially-weighted moving average over 1–5 minutes.
- estimated_future_qps: simple recency predictor + sticky-session weight (session-id present?).
- estimated_migration_cost: bytes to copy and number of active in-flight decodes referencing that prefix.
- Hot-prefix threshold: choose thresholds dynamically to capture 80th percentile of traffic using Pareto estimates.
- Top-K per shard: keep K=500–2000 depending on model and shard size (configurable).

KV population mechanics:
- Two copy modes:
  1) local-ssd snapshot copy: write hotspot prefixes to local SSD of target GPU node via an ordered atomic update. Used when cross-node bandwidth constrained or when priorities are lower.
  2) NVLink direct peer-copy: use nvpeer APIs when source and target GPUs share NVLink; this is faster and should be used for hot prefixes.
- Copy protocol must be idempotent and support resume. Use generation tags: (model_version, request_epoch, prefix_id) to guard against duplicate/old writes.
- Install semantics: write-then-atomic-swap pointer so ongoing decodes either use old or new location cleanly.

NCCL and network heuristics (tuning knobs):
- Separate control plane for rebalancing traffic: avoid interfering with collective traffic used for decoding. Implement QoS at runtime: mark rebalancing copies with lower priority, and use NCCL streams or verbs with throttling.
- Tune NCCL collective algorithms based on size: small (<= 64KB) per-chunk favors ring; large favors tree/recursive doubling. Use adaptive selection based on observed per-chunk latency and throughput.
- Limit concurrent collective count per NIC to avoid queueing; set max_concurrent_collectives per node (configurable; default 4).
- For inter-node copies, prefer RDMA (if available) over CPU-relay; use direct GPUDirect where supported.

Scheduler integration and routing policy changes:
- Routing layer must be aware of placement metadata with two states per shard: primary_location + copy_state (LOCAL | REPLICATING | STALE | MIGRATED).
- For lazy mode, route to new owner for new requests (so compute is balanced) but use remote-KV-on-demand RPCs to old owners until copy_state == LOCAL on new owner.
- SLO guardrails: if background rebalancing increases p99 by more than threshold, automatically slow prefetch and reduce max_concurrent_collectives.
- Backpressure: when network utilization above X% or NVLink error rates spike, shift to conservative copy mode (local-ssd snapshot) and increase lazy fetches.

Micro-batching and kernel implications:
- Continuous batching (our runtime's typical decode path) aggregates many requests; remote KV hits become vectorizable if we batch remote fetches. Implement a remote-KV fetch aggregator per-shard that groups outstanding remote-key reads into one batched RPC to reduce overhead.
- Kernel fusion: prefer fused KV read + attention kernel for local reads. When remote fetch occurs, fallback to split path: remote fetch + fused attention once KV available. This imposes a code-path divergence cost—prefer to prefetch hot prefixes to avoid divergence.

Metrics and observability (must be tracked):
- resharding_bandwidth_used (GB/s) per node
- concurrent_rebalancing_operations
- remote_kv_latency p50/p95/p99 (ms)
- rebalancing_p99_inflation_ratio (compare windowed p99 vs baseline)
- hot_prefix_hit_rate (fraction of hot requests served locally)
- nvlink_utilization, pci_utilization, nic_rx/tx_bytes
- copy_failures / aborts / resumptions

Experiment plan (short-term prototypes):
1) Implement lazy-on-demand remote fetch path + batched remote-KV aggregator. Run against replay workload for the model in JIRA-RT-1987. Measure p50/p99 overhead for cold requests and hot_prefix_hit_rate after 10 minutes.
2) Add simple EWMA hot-prefix scorer and background NVLink peer-copy for top-500 per shard. Introduce max_concurrent_collectives=2. Re-run scale-up scenario and measure p99 inflation.
3) Add adaptive NCCL algorithm selector based on chunk size; compare against baseline NCCL config.
4) Simulate node preemption (sudden removal) and measure time-to-stabilize (time until 95% requests served locally at new placement) and tail latency.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How to bound memory blowup during aggressive replication? Need admission control for replication.
- Cost model for proactive replication vs remote fetch latency: where to put break-even point? (depends on customer SLOs and traffic skew).
- Does NVSwitch vs NVLink vs IB topology require per-cluster default heuristics? Likely yes—maintain topology profile detected at startup.
- Can we leverage model-specific structure to shard prefixes more intelligently (e.g., by attention locality) rather than contiguous tensor ranges?

Next steps / action items:
- [Maya] prototype batched remote-KV fetch aggregator (2 weeks)
- [Liam] add basic EWMA hot-prefix scorer and top-K replication loop, integrate NVLink copy path (3 weeks)
- [Priya] create experiment harness and traffic replay for JIRA-RT-1987 incident (1 week)
- [Diego] add NCCL knobbed config flags and ability to switch collective algorithm at runtime (2 weeks)
- Sync with SRE to add observability dashboards for the metrics above before enabling background replication on any production fleet.

Appendix: micro-protocol sketch for batched remote-KV fetch:
1) Aggregator receives N remote read requests for prefixes {p1..pN} targeting shard S.
2) Deduplicate prefix ids and build a vectorized fetch request with per-prefix byte ranges.
3) Send as single RDMA/RPC with a small header (target model_version, epoch).
4) Source shard responds with contiguous blob + per-prefix offsets.
5) Aggregator unpacks and forwards per-request KV frames into awaiting decode contexts.
6) If any prefix missing at source (evicted), return "MISS" and fall back to cold-path load-from-object-store.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a sketch mixing low-level and high-level ideas; prefer to iterate via small experiments rather than finalize heavy invariants up-front.
- Feedback requested on the hot-prefix scoring formula (alpha/beta/gamma defaults) and acceptable defaults for max_concurrent_collectives by topology.
